questions.q: In a linear programming problem, the feasible region is:
questions.solution:
The feasible region is where **every** constraint holds at once — the overlap of all the shaded half-planes.

It is the set of plans you are actually allowed to carry out; the objective function only comes in afterwards, to rank them.
options: the set of all points satisfying the objective function
the common region of all the constraints

questions.q: If a linear programming problem has an optimal solution over a bounded feasible region, that optimum occurs:
questions.solution:
A linear objective function has no peaks in the middle — it slides steadily across the region, so its best value is pushed out to the boundary and, in the end, to a **corner point**.

Tilt a tray of marbles: they all end up in a corner, never in the middle.
options: at the centre of the region
at a corner point of the region

questions.q: Which of these points satisfies $x + y \le 4$, $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$?
questions.solution:
Test each: $(3,2)$ gives $5 > 4$ ✗; $(-1,1)$ breaks $x \ge 0$ ✗; $(5,0)$ gives $5 > 4$ ✗.

$(1, 2)$ gives $3 \le 4$ and both coordinates non-negative. ✓

questions.q: If the feasible region of an LPP is unbounded, then the objective function:
questions.solution:
An unbounded region stretches away forever in some direction, and an objective function that grows in that direction never stops growing — so a **maximum may not exist**.

The standard test: a maximum claimed at a corner is genuine only if the open half-plane $Z > $ (that value) has no point of the feasible region in it.

questions.q: In every linear programming problem in the Class 12 syllabus, the constraints $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$ are present because:
questions.solution:
$x$ and $y$ stand for numbers of chairs, kilograms of fertiliser, hours of machine time — none of which can be negative.

They are called the **non-negativity constraints**, and they come from the real problem, not from the mathematics.
options: they make the graph easier to draw
the variables represent quantities that cannot be negative
they are required by the corner point theorem

questions.q: The corner points of a feasible region are $(0,0)$, $(4,0)$, $(3,2)$ and $(0,3)$. Find the maximum value of $Z = 5x + 3y$.
questions.solution:
Evaluate $Z$ at every corner:

$(0,0) \to 0$; $(4,0) \to 20$; $(3,2) \to 15 + 6 = 21$; $(0,3) \to 9$.

Maximum $= \mathbf{21}$ at $(3, 2)$.

Four arithmetic lines and the answer is settled — that is the whole power of the corner point theorem.

questions.q: For the same corner points $(0,0)$, $(4,0)$, $(3,2)$, $(0,3)$, find the minimum value of $Z = 2x + 7y$.
questions.solution:
$(0,0) \to 0$; $(4,0) \to 8$; $(3,2) \to 20$; $(0,3) \to 21$.

Minimum $= \mathbf{0}$ at the origin.

When both coefficients are positive and the origin is feasible, the origin always wins the minimum.

questions.q: Find the value of $Z = x + y$ at the point where $x + 2y = 10$ meets $2x + y = 10$.
questions.solution:
Adding the equations: $3x + 3y = 20 \Rightarrow x + y = \dfrac{20}{3} \approx \mathbf{6.667}$.

No need to find $x$ and $y$ separately — the objective function asked only for their sum. Looking for that shortcut is worth a few seconds in an exam.

questions.q: How many corner points does the feasible region $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$, $x + y \le 5$ have?
questions.solution:
The region is the triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(5,0)$ and $(0,5)$ — $\mathbf{3}$ corner points.

Sketching the region first, however roughly, is always faster than reasoning about it in the abstract.

questions.q: Maximise $Z = 4x + y$ subject to $x + y \le 5$, $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$. Give the maximum value.
questions.solution:
Corners: $(0,0) \to 0$; $(5,0) \to 20$; $(0,5) \to 5$.

Maximum $= \mathbf{20}$ at $(5, 0)$.

$x$ is worth four times as much as $y$ per unit and costs the same in the constraint, so everything goes into $x$.

questions.q: Maximise $Z = 3x + 4y$ subject to $x + y \le 4$, $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$. Show the corner points you used.
questions.solution:
**The region.** $x + y \le 4$ with both variables non-negative is the triangle $(0,0)$, $(4,0)$, $(0,4)$ — bounded, so a maximum certainly exists.

**Evaluate $Z = 3x + 4y$ at each corner:**

$(0,0) \to 0$

$(4,0) \to 12$

$(0,4) \to 16$

**Maximum $= 16$ at $(0, 4)$.**

Each unit of the budget buys $4$ if spent on $y$ and only $3$ if spent on $x$, and both cost the same — so the whole budget goes to $y$.

questions.q: A shopkeeper makes two kinds of gift box. Box A needs 2 hours of labour and returns ₹30 profit; Box B needs 3 hours and returns ₹40. There are 60 hours of labour available and at most 25 boxes can be sold in total. Formulate this as a linear programming problem.
questions.solution:
**Decision variables.** Let $x$ = number of Box A and $y$ = number of Box B.

**Objective.** Maximise $Z = 30x + 40y$ (profit in rupees).

**Constraints.**

Labour: $2x + 3y \le 60$

Sales: $x + y \le 25$

Non-negativity: $x \ge 0,\; y \ge 0$

Formulating is three questions in order: what am I choosing, what am I trying to make big, and what is stopping me. Each line of the problem becomes exactly one of those.

**Corner points.** The boundary lines are $2x + 3y = 60$ and $x + y = 25$.

They meet where $2x + 3(25 - x) = 60 \Rightarrow 75 - x = 60 \Rightarrow x = 15$, $y = 10$.

Also on the axes: $x + y = 25$ meets the $x$-axis at $(25, 0)$, but that fails $2x + 3y \le 60$ ($50 \le 60$ ✓ — it is feasible).

And $2x + 3y = 60$ meets the $y$-axis at $(0, 20)$, which satisfies $x + y \le 25$. ✓

So the corners are $(0,0)$, $(25,0)$, $(15,10)$ and $(0,20)$.

**Evaluate $Z = 60x + 40y$:**

$(0,0) \to 0$; $(25,0) \to 1500$; $(15,10) \to 900 + 400 = 1300$; $(0,20) \to 800$.

**Maximum $= 1500$ at $(25, 0)$.**

The intersection point is not always the winner — it has to be checked against the axis corners like any other.

questions.q: Minimise $Z = 3x + 5y$ subject to $x + y \ge 2$, $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$, and explain why the answer is trustworthy even though the region is unbounded.
questions.solution:
The corner points of this unbounded region are $(2, 0)$ and $(0, 2)$.

$Z(2,0) = 6$ and $Z(0,2) = 10$, so the candidate minimum is $6$.

**The check for an unbounded region:** does $3x + 5y < 6$ contain any feasible point?

On the feasible region $x + y \ge 2$, and since $3x + 5y \ge 3(x + y) \ge 6$, no feasible point can beat $6$.

**Minimum $= 6$ at $(2, 0)$.**

For an unbounded region the corner values are only candidates until that half-plane test is done — and a *minimum* with positive coefficients is the case that usually survives it.

questions.q: An LPP in $x$ (tables) and $y$ (chairs) has its maximum profit at the corner point $(7.5,\; 12)$. Explain what a manufacturer should actually do.
questions.solution:
The mathematics is right but the answer is not usable: you cannot make half a table.

The feasible **integer** points nearby have to be tested — $(7, 12)$ and, if it satisfies every constraint, $(8, 12)$ — and whichever gives the larger profit **while remaining feasible** is the plan.

A corner point may be fractional; the recommendation must not be. (Problems where the variables must be whole numbers are called integer programming, and they are genuinely harder — which is why Class 12 problems are set so the corner comes out whole.)
